60K+ healthcare professionals and patients on the ZoomRx panel; the survey platform is its daily surface

ZoomRx runs market research on healthcare professionals, physicians whose time is expensive, whose patience is short, and whose honest answers are the entire product. When I took on the survey experience, nothing measured it: feedback arrived by email, and nobody owned it. So the first thing I built was the measure itself, the Net Promoter Score (NPS) system, kept in an Excel sheet at first and later turned, with AI, into a dashboard anyone could open. Its first reading, in November 2024, was −13: respondents telling us, in the most direct metric that exists, that taking our surveys was a bad experience. By early 2026, NPS was +44, a 57-point swing. None of that was one redesign; it was a sustained programme of experience work: Reducing cognitive load, question by question Rebuilding the feedback loops Fixing onboarding Building a design system that could hold quality steady across more than 1,000 live surveys

The measurement program linked detractor feedback to design sprints and contributed to NPS moving from −13 in November 2024 to +44 by early 2026. The NPS question and the end-of-survey feedback (EOSF) together collected 30,000+ structured responses. Patient Load completion rates increased by 24%; onboarding work grew monthly active users from ~400 to ~550 (+38%) and improved 90-day retention by ~19%.

p.s: 02 The world this product lives in
p.x: To judge the decisions you need the vocabulary they were made in. Healthcare market research is its own world; here is the plain-language version of the nine terms this case study leans on. HCP panel A standing community of healthcare professionals (physicians, mostly) who take paid market-research surveys for pharma clients. ZoomRx's panel is 60K+ HCPs and patients; the survey platform is where they meet it every day. Panelist A verified member of the panel. Identity is checked against a work email and an ID document before surveys unlock, because a research panel is only worth what its members' identities are worth. Honorarium What a physician is paid for a survey. It sits on every survey tile with the time estimate and "what you'll do", so taking a survey is an informed decision, not a gamble. LOI Length of interview: how long a survey says it will take, shown on its tile beside the honorarium. The usability study found surveys running longer than their advertised LOI, a broken promise to a physician who picked the survey partly on that number. Screen-out

p.s: 02 The world this product lives in
p.x: The qualification questions at the start of a study decide whether a respondent is eligible. Being screened out after fifteen minutes of qualifiers was the most-quoted frustration in the usability study. Patient Load The yearly onboarding survey every panelist completes about their practice. Its completion rate is one of the four numbers that moved: +24% year on year after the redesign. EOSF End-of-Survey Feedback: a two-step prompt at the moment a survey is completed, a recommendation score, then named areas of the experience to agree or disagree with. 30,000+ responses together with the NPS question; the programme's evidence base. NPS Net Promoter Score, from one question: "how likely are you to recommend us?", answered 0 to 10. Promoters answer 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8, detractors 0 to 6. The score is the share of promoters minus the share of detractors, so it runs from −100 to +100; passives count toward the total but neither add nor subtract. The platform's running measure: from −13 in November 2024 to +44 by early 2026. SUS

p.s: 02 The world this product lives in
p.x: System Usability Scale: a ten-question standard score where 68 is the benchmark. The study's SUS was 85, reassuring, and it hid the problem.

A survey platform has an unusual property: its users are also its supply chain. If physicians dislike the experience, they respond less, answer worse, and eventually leave the panel, and the company's product (research data) degrades with them. When the first NPS reading came back at −13, it wasn't a vanity-metric problem; it was a leading indicator of supply risk. Demand for respondents had been growing faster than the panel, and the survey experience is where panelists spend nearly all of their time with ZoomRx, so the experience was the lever that decided whether the panel kept up. The experience problems were structural. Surveys were long and cognitively expensive, dense grids, repetitive patterns, unclear progress. There was no systematic way to hear what respondents thought at the moment they finished. And with over a thousand live surveys authored across teams, quality varied wildly, the experience depended on who had built the survey, not on a system.

Design challenge. How might we make surveys that busy physicians don't dread, at a scale where no individual screen can be hand-polished? p.s: 04 Research: the study that started it
p.x: The study that started it. Before any redesign, we sat with the people taking the surveys. Eight panel physicians, oncologists and haematologists, were recruited for one-hour moderated remote sessions at a $300 honorarium and taken through a discussion guide and four task scenarios on the live app: sign-up, two survey flows, and the auxiliary flows around them. Every session was recorded; we measured errors, time and satisfaction per task and collected a System Usability Scale score.

p.s: 04 Research: the study that started it
p.x: Two kinds of numbers came out of it, and they disagreed. At the end of each session, participants filled in the System Usability Scale, a standard ten-question score out of 100 for how easy an app is to use. The median was 85, well above the 68 that counts as good, so on that score alone the app passed. The task timings said something else: the two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes each, averaged 1.4 to 1.6 errors, and were rated the least satisfying of the four tasks (5.3 out of 7). In plain terms, the shell of the app, its sign-up, navigation and account screens, worked well; the surveys inside it did not. The overall score was averaging the good part with the bad part, and hiding the bad part. That gap is the whole case study. THE STUDY · AS RUN, NOT AS PLANNED Method Moderated usability study: one-hour remote sessions on the live app, with a discussion guide and four task scenarios, sign-up, two survey flows, and the auxiliary flows around them. Three things kept surfacing: in the sessions, in the task metrics and in the live surveys. Each one is tagged with where it was read from, and each became a decision. 01

p.u: The feedback had to come from the moment, not the memory
p.x: The feedback had to come from the moment, not the memory. Asking respondents later what they thought produces politeness. Asking at the instant they finish a survey, while the friction is fresh, produces the truth. The End of Survey Feedback (EOSF) mechanism became the engine of the whole programme: 30,000+ responses, with the NPS question, that turned redesign priorities from opinion into evidence. How we knew Before the study there was no channel at all: panelists wrote emails, and with nobody owning them the emails went unanswered. Eight one-hour sessions were the first time the team sat with respondents, and what they said in the moment made the case for a permanent prompt at the end of every survey. → Decision 1 Read from 8 moderated sessions · the feedback emails nobody owned 02

p.u: Cognitive load is the real completion tax
p.x: Cognitive load is the real completion tax. Drop-off didn't correlate with survey length as much as with density, the grids, the repeated matrices, the screens that demanded re-reading. Reducing effort-per-question mattered more than reducing questions. How we knew Task-based testing first: the two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes each with 1.4–1.6 errors and the lowest satisfaction (5.3 of 7) against a SUS of 85, the burden was in the questions, not the app. Then drop-off analysis across live surveys: completion fell with grid density and repeated matrices far more than with question count. → Decision 2 Read from errors, time and satisfaction per task · drop-off analysis by survey density 03

p.u: At 1,000+ surveys, the system is the design
p.x: At 1,000+ surveys, the system is the design. No team can hand-polish a thousand live instruments. Past a certain scale, the only way to raise experience quality is to raise the floor, tokens, patterns, and question templates that make the good version the default version. How we knew The study’s first finding: nobody owned how questions were formatted, a survey went from the consulting team’s draft to a coded instrument with no design step in between. Over a thousand live surveys had been authored that way, with quality varying by author. → Decision 3 Read from study finding 1: nobody owned question design · the 1,000-survey inventory

p.u: Decision 1: Build the feedback loop before the redesign
p.x: Decision 1: Build the feedback loop before the redesign. What we saw No channel existed. Panelists wrote emails, nobody owned them, and the eight sessions were the first time the team had sat with respondents. What we did Built the NPS and End-of-Survey Feedback system myself before redesigning anything, a score at completion, then a reason; an Excel sheet first, later a dashboard built with AI, and prioritised every sprint after from it. The EOSF programme came first, deliberately. Redesigning on intuition risked optimising the wrong friction; 30,000+ responses meant every subsequent change had evidence behind it and a measurement after it. Tradeoff: slower visible progress at the start, a quarter spent instrumenting instead of shipping screens. It converted the rest of the programme from guesswork to compounding.

p.u: Decision 1: Build the feedback loop before the redesign
p.x: The feedback data had a second life. The End-of-Survey Feedback and the emails before it kept raising the same questions: a survey link that would not open, a bonus that had not arrived, an account problem. So I designed and vibe-coded Zena, a support agent that lives on the dashboard: a panelist asks from the point they are stuck, Zena finds the survey, answers what it can about payments and surveys, and turns the rest into a ticket with the conversation attached. Its own card in More projects has the quick case study.

p.u: Decision 2: Attack cognitive load, not survey length
p.x: Decision 2: Attack cognitive load, not survey length. What we saw The two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes with 1.4–1.6 errors; across live surveys, completion fell with grid density far more than with question count. What we did Targeted effort per question: simplified patterns, visible progress, dense grids broken into sequenced steps. The redesign targeted effort-per-question: simplified interaction patterns, clearer progress, breaking dense grids into sequenced steps. Tradeoff: sequencing dense questions adds screens and can lengthen perceived duration, the bet was that lighter screens beat fewer screens. The NPS trajectory and the 24% increase in Patient Load completion rates backed it.

p.u: Decision 2: Attack cognitive load, not survey length
p.x: Patient Load is where this decision is easiest to see. It is the yearly onboarding survey every panelist completes, and it had been losing completions year on year. The recording walks through the dense version first, then what we changed: guidelines before the first question, five steps by tumour group, indications chosen before the lines of therapy are asked for each one, and a visible path through all of it. Completion rose 24% year on year.

p.u: Decision 3: A design system sized for survey authors, not designers
p.x: Decision 3: A design system sized for survey authors, not designers. What we saw Nobody owned how questions were formatted; a thousand-plus surveys had been authored that way, quality varying by author. What we did A design system sized for survey authors: 200+ components, tokens and question templates that make the good version the default, no designer in the loop required. The system's real users were the people building surveys at volume. It had to make the right pattern the easy pattern, templates and components that produce consistent experience without a designer in the loop. The system's rules are written doctrine, starting with its first principle: the physician is the hero; ZoomRx is the tool. Its discipline runs to the pixel, at one point, four visually indistinguishable navy variants that had drifted into production were consolidated into a single brand navy, on the record, with a date.

p.u: Decision 3: A design system sized for survey authors, not designers
p.x: The Figma design system contains 200+ components, design tokens and WCAG 2.1 AA patterns for 1,000+ surveys across web and mobile. Its token architecture links primitive values to semantic roles and components; the source inventory also includes 439 icons and 249 illustrations. Later, the same system became the foundation for agent-generated screens, see the Boilerplate Generator case study. Tradeoff: systematising removes flexibility, and some studies genuinely need bespoke instruments. The system had to leave escape hatches without letting the escape hatch become the norm. p.u: Decision 4: Onboarding as retention work, verification as trust work
p.x: Decision 4: Onboarding as retention work, verification as trust work. What we saw Amplitude funnel and cohort analysis on new panelists, framed with Jobs-to-be-Done; and a panel whose value rests on verified identities. What we did Redesigned onboarding around the jobs; verification with a work email from a persistent banner, surveys held blurred until the account is active. Onboarding was redesigned using Jobs-to-be-Done and Amplitude funnel/cohort analysis. Monthly active users grew from ~400 to ~550 (+38%), and 90-day retention improved by ~19%. Identity also became part of the design: panelists verify with their work email and complete identity verification from a persistent dashboard banner, with surveys held blurred until the account is activated. Tradeoff: verification gates add friction exactly where drop-off hurts most, at the door. But a research panel is only worth what its members' identities are worth: the friction buys the integrity the entire product is sold on.

p.u: Decision 5: Never dead-end a willing respondent
p.x: Decision 5: Never dead-end a willing respondent. What we saw "Fifteen to twenty minutes of qualifications and then sorry, you don't qualify", the most-quoted frustration in the sessions. What we did Every exit leads somewhere: finish → earnings and the next study; screened out → an apology with alternatives; home → the next opportunity waiting. The survey loop is designed by scenario, and every exit leads somewhere: finish a survey and see your earnings and the next study ("Earn $75 more"); get screened out and land on an apology that immediately offers alternatives; head home and find the next opportunity waiting. A respondent with time and willingness is the scarcest asset the platform has; the design refuses to waste one. Tradeoff: chaining opportunities risks feeling like a content treadmill. Pay, time estimates, and "what you'll do" sit on every tile so each next step is an informed choice, not an infinite scroll.

The panelist's world. The dashboard is a working professional's earning surface, and it reads like one: survey tiles carry pay, time estimate, and "what you'll do" up front (respect for the respondent's decision, tile by tile) with early-access badges, guaranteed-pay variants, and honest unavailable states ("available again on…"). A verification banner tracks identity status at the top, and the platform's other faces sit one tab away: Surveys, Playground, Briefs.

Worth opening between surveys. A panel that only hears from you when you want data is a panel that stops answering. The platform earns visits between studies: clinical and case polls with community results, quizzes with explained answers, and the Playground, light engagement that keeps the habit alive without cheapening the professional context.

p.x: One ecosystem, visible in one screen. The dashboard quietly connects the portfolio: a $30 AI-moderated interview tile on it is Sagan, the interviewer I designed, being fielded through the survey platform, and the Briefs tab is Curie's content inside the panelist's daily surface. Three products from this portfolio, one screen.

Four directions were on the table and were not taken. Each one was the easier build. Redesign first, measure later. The instinct every team has when a number is bad. Redesigning on intuition risked optimising the wrong friction; the feedback loop came first and cost a quarter. Shorten the surveys. Drop-off tracked density, not question count. The bet was that lighter screens beat fewer screens, and the studies kept the questions they needed. A design system for designers. No designer was in the loop for most of a thousand surveys. The system had to make the right pattern the easy pattern for the people building at volume. End at a thank-you page. A respondent with time and willingness is the scarcest asset the platform has. Every exit now leads to a next step.

p.x: From a one-off study to a standing channel. The study was a one-off, and the thing it made obvious was that nothing continuous existed. Panelists had been writing emails; with nobody owning them, the emails went unanswered. So the first thing I built was the End-of-Survey Feedback prompt and the NPS system behind it, a recommendation score at the moment of completion, then a second step naming the areas of the experience to agree or disagree with, so a detractor score arrives with a reason. The boards carry the iteration record: tile states, verification flows and the survey loop exist in versioned explorations. Gribb's platform starts with a piece of hardware: a Geotab telematics device installed in delivery vehicles. It reports, live, how each vehicle is being driven, harsh braking, sudden acceleration, hard turns, idling, and more. For the delivery companies running these fleets, DHL and UPS among them, that stream holds the answers to expensive questions. Raw, it's unreadable. As Lead Designer over 18 months, I designed both sides of that translation: the dashboard that fleet clients, insurers, and resellers used to understand every vehicle, driver, and trip, and the driver app that turned safe driving into a score worth competing for, with real rewards behind it. The honest scope of this product is large: multi-tenant client management, a configurable rule engine, fleet analytics, fuel economics, exception maps, shift management, damage reporting, driver gamification. The design job was to make sure no single user ever felt that size: A driver sees a score and a game A manager sees their fleet and what needs attention An insurer sees risk and evidence
The complexity lives in the system; the simplicity lives in each person's slice of it: keeping that separation was the work.

A fleet operator cares about a small number of questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, and where the operation is losing money. The Geotab device answers all of them, but in the form of thousands of raw data points per vehicle per day. No operations manager at a delivery company reads telemetry, and no driver changes how they brake because a sensor logged an event. The gap between what the device knew and what a client could act on: that gap was the product.

Design challenge. How might we turn one live telemetry stream into something two very different audiences act on, managers making decisions about their fleet, and drivers making decisions behind the wheel?

Told from both seats: the manager's and the driver's. Same telemetry, two working lives. WHO I DESIGNED FOR · TWO SEATS, ONE ENGINE · ROLES, NOT INVENTED PEOPLE A fleet operations manager at a delivery company runs vehicles, drivers and shifts for a client such as DHL or UPS · answers to the operation and to its insurer · opens the dashboard first thing in the morning A delivery driver on a shared fleet starts a route on whichever van is free · judged by a score built from the device in the vehicle · rewarded, in gift cards, on how that score reads Goals Have anything wrong already in front of me when I open the dashboard, so I can act before the shift starts See the trips and events behind a score, so I can defend it to the driver or correct it Know whether the fleet is getting better, not only who needs attention today Start a shift in seconds, without fighting a form See my score and why it is what it is, on the trip, in the app Stand somewhere against people I actually know, and have safe driving be worth something Frustrations

How might we…. HMW 1 turn one live telemetry stream into something two very different audiences act on, managers about their fleet and drivers behind the wheel? HMW 2 let a client define safe driving for its own roads, vehicles and weather, without a redesign for each one? HMW 3 make a score that judges people one they can contest, and still believe? HMW 4 make safe driving visible and worth something to the driver, not only to the manager? HMW 5 bind a driver to a shared vehicle in seconds, so per-driver scoring is possible at all?

Fleet telematics has its own vocabulary, and the decisions below were made in it. The plain-language version of the eight terms this case study leans on. Geotab device A telematics unit installed in each delivery vehicle. It reports, live, how the vehicle is being driven: harsh braking, sudden acceleration, hard turns, idling and more. Thousands of data points per vehicle per day. Event One thing the device noticed: a harsh-braking spike, a collision, idling past a threshold. People respond to events; nobody watches the stream they come from. Exception An event the rules decided was worth a manager’s attention. Exceptions surface on the dashboard and on a map; ordinary operation stays quiet. Rule engine Where events become a score. Every rule carries context: the same harsh braking scores differently on a snowy night in a truck than on a dry highway in a van. Road type, vehicle category, day versus night and weather are live, weighted inputs, and each client sets them from its own admin. Driving score

The number the rule engine produces per driver, vehicle, trip and shift. Legible by design: every point traces back to a named rule, which is what lets a manager defend it and a driver contest it. Query A driver’s appeal against an exception, raised from the app with their case stated. The manager reviews the trip and marks it valid or invalid; valid queries correct the record. Shift The unit everything on the driver’s side hangs off. It starts with a scan of the vehicle’s number plate, which binds driver to vehicle and makes per-driver scoring possible on shared fleets. Risk band How a fleet is summarised for clients and their insurers: a weekly behaviour report that bands the fleet by risk, with exports and scheduled emails behind it.

What we found Managers and drivers needed the same data for opposite reasons. People respond to events, not streams. What it became One data model with two faces (Decision 1), a rule engine configured by each client (Decision 2), due process for the score (Decision 3) and gamification with real stakes (Decision 4). Three things held across 18 months of releases. Each one is tagged with where it was read from, and each became a decision or a rule the whole product follows. 01

p.u: Managers and drivers need the same data for opposite reasons
p.x: Managers and drivers need the same data for opposite reasons. A fleet manager looks at driving behaviour to hold the operation accountable. A driver looks at it to know how they're doing. One audience needs oversight; the other needs motivation. Designing one interface for both would have served neither, the data had to wear two faces. How we knew Worked out with Gribb’s CTO from the two audiences’ jobs, the client’s fleet managers, who have to hold the operation accountable, and the drivers being held to it, and borne out by every release after: a metric added to the engine landed on both sides without rework. → Decision 1 Read from the two audiences’ jobs, worked out with the CTO · every release after 02

Events matter more than streams. Nobody watches telemetry. People respond to things that happen, a collision, a harsh-braking spike, a vehicle trending toward a fault. The dashboard had to surface events and exceptions instantly and let ordinary operation stay quiet. How we knew The raw feed itself, thousands of data points per vehicle per day that no operations manager reads, and what clients were paying for: to know when something happened, not to watch a stream. → the alert and exception model Read from the raw Geotab feed · what clients were paying for 03

p.u: A score only changes driving if drivers accept it
p.x: A score only changes driving if drivers accept it. A driving score changes conversations between managers and drivers, and drivers push back on numbers they can't trace. The score had to be legible (built from named events like harsh braking and idling, through rules anyone could understand) before it could be motivating. Gamification only works on top of a score people believe. How we knew Anticipated with the CTO when the score was defined, a number that judges people invites pushback, then confirmed in the field: every query a driver raised was a case where the score did not match the road. → Decision 3 Read from the score definition, with the CTO · driver queries in the field

The two hardest problems of the project sat next to each other: defining the rule engine, deciding how driving would be judged at all, and designing a dashboard that could hold this much product without collapsing. The gamification system and the plate-scan check-in were hard in a different way: they had to make sophisticated machinery feel effortless to the person using it.

p.u: Decision 1: One data model, two faces
p.x: Decision 1: One data model, two faces. The manager’s seat Answers the manager’s questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, what the fleet looks like tonight. Framed for accountability. The driver’s seat Answers the driver’s: how am I doing, where do I stand, what’s my score. Framed for motivation, and always the same score the manager sees. The client dashboard and the driver app were designed as one system serving opposite needs. The dashboard answers the manager's questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, what does the fleet look like tonight. The app answers the driver's: how am I doing, where do I stand, what's my score. Same telemetry, same rule engine, opposite framing. Tradeoff: one coherent system is slower to design upfront than two independent products. It paid back constantly: every metric added to the rule engine appeared on both sides without rework, and the score a manager saw always matched the score a driver was chasing.

p.u: Decision 2: Configuration over customisation: the rule engine
p.x: Decision 2: Configuration over customisation: the rule engine. The manager’s seat Each client sets the weights for road type, vehicle category, day or night and weather from its own admin, so the product holds its own definition of safe driving without a redesign. The driver’s seat The same brake is not the same brake: a harsh stop on a snowy night in a truck is not scored like one on a dry highway in a van, and every point traces to a named rule. We didn't hard-code what "bad driving" means, because it doesn't mean one thing. Behaviour events flowed through a rule engine where every rule carries context: the same harsh braking scores differently on a snowy night in a truck than on a dry highway in a van. Road type, vehicle category, day versus night and weather were all live inputs, weighted, and configured by each client themselves from their own admin, down to the score bands and the colours that represent them.

p.u: Decision 2: Configuration over customisation: the rule engine
p.x: Tradeoff: building the engine before the interface cost time when nothing visual existed to show for it, and every configurable option is a screen an admin has to understand. But it meant one product could serve every client's definition of safe driving without redesign, and the score stayed explainable, because every point traced back to a named rule.

p.u: Decision 3: Due process for the algorithm
p.x: Decision 3: Due process for the algorithm. The manager’s seat Reviews the trip behind a query and marks it valid or invalid. The pattern of queries shows where the scoring feels wrong to the people being scored. The driver’s seat Can query any exception from the app and state the case: the speed limit was different, the idling had a reason. Valid queries correct the record. A score that judges people needs a way to be wrong. If a driver believed an exception was unfair (the speed limit was different, the idling had a reason) they could raise a query from the app, state their case, and have it land with their manager, who reviews the trip and marks the query valid or invalid. Valid queries correct the record. Tradeoff: an appeals process invites appeals, it costs manager time and admits the system makes mistakes. We took that cost deliberately: a contestable score gets trusted and a black box gets gamed. The dispute flow is what let the same number carry a manager's judgement and a driver's pay-adjacent rewards without being resented.

Decision 4: Gamification with real stakes. The manager’s seat Gets a score drivers try to improve instead of resent, and one that is hard to game, because the rules are context-aware and every point can be contested. The driver’s seat Levels, streaks and milestones; leaderboards against people in the same hub; 30-second lessons that earn points; coins redeemed for real gift cards. Surveillance data has a dignity problem: a system that only reports drivers to their managers gets resented and gamed. So the driver app flipped the framing. The score became a progression system (levels, streaks, milestones) with leaderboards ranked against people drivers actually know ("best 5% in your hub", not an anonymous global list), 30-second improvement lessons that themselves earn points, and coins that redeem into real Amazon gift cards. Tradeoff: paying for scores invites chasing scores. The counterweight was the rule engine's context-awareness and the dispute flow, a score that's fair and explainable is hard to cheat and worth winning.

What we didn’t build. Two independent products. The obvious split: a dashboard for clients, an app for drivers. One coherent system was slower to design up front and paid back constantly: every metric added to the rule engine appeared on both sides without rework. One universal definition of bad driving. The same thresholds for every client, vehicle and weather condition. Far simpler to build, and wrong everywhere except the average case. A score with no appeal. A black box is cheaper than a dispute flow and gets gamed. A contestable score costs manager time and admits mistakes, and gets trusted. Reporting-only telemetry. The obvious MVP: data flowing one way, upward to managers. It would have made the app the driver’s enemy from the first day. An anonymous global leaderboard. Ranking drivers against strangers motivates nobody. The leaderboards rank against people drivers actually know: the best 5% in your hub.

p.s: 08 User flows: the app and the dashboard
p.x: The two products as people move through them. The driver’s flow hangs off the shift and ends in the game loop; the manager’s starts from whatever is wrong and drills down to a single event. The query is where the two flows meet.

The shift is the spine. The driver's seat. On the driver's side, everything hangs off one unit: the shift. Check-in by scanning the vehicle's number plate, the camera does the work, because a driver starting a route shouldn't be fighting a form. The check-in binds driver to vehicle, which is what makes per-driver scoring possible at all on shared fleets. Then the pre-vehicle safety check, the scored trips, any damage reports (tap the vehicle diagram where the damage is, add photos), and check-out. Each shift closes with its own score, its own condition record, its own paper trail, one driver, one vehicle, one accountable session.

p.u: The dashboard reads outward from the same spine
p.x: The dashboard reads outward from the same spine. The manager's seat. Fleet overview → vehicles → drivers → trips → exceptions, each level opening into the one below, down to a single braking event on a map. Around that core: live fleet map, fuel economics, score comparison between any two groups or periods, and reporting that leaves the building, exports, scheduled emails, and a designed weekly behaviour report that risk-bands the fleet for clients and insurers.

How every screen behaves. Two rules governed the whole product: Problems find the manager, not the other way around. Open the dashboard and anything wrong is already in front of you; serious incidents interrupt with an alert, and everything running normally stays quietly in the background. Every number opens up. Tap a score and see the trips behind it; tap a trip and see the events behind that. Nothing on screen is a dead end. The same two rules hold on the driver's side: the score is always one glance away, and tapping it always shows you why it is what it is.

p.s: 11 What shipped, and where it went
p.x: Release by release. The product shipped in versions (Drivers v2 and v3, Trips V2, Check-in/out V2, Reporting v3) and went through a full rebrand along the way. Design here wasn't a phase before build; it was an 18-month loop of launching, getting feedback, and revising. The versions themselves show what that feedback taught us: Check-in/out V2 added CSV shift imports and let managers create a check-in on a driver's behalf, because real shifts don't always start in the app. Drivers forget, and the record still has to be right. Drivers v3 put a fleet-wide score trend graph above the driver list, managers weren't only asking "who needs attention today", they were asking "are we getting better?" Reporting v3 went day-wise: weekly numbers were too coarse for clients who wanted to see the effect of a change that same week. Two feedback channels were also built into the product itself: Driver queries: every disputed exception told us exactly where the scoring felt wrong to the people being scored. The people most affected by the system were also its most honest testers.

p.s: 11 What shipped, and where it went
p.x: The trip-lifecycle report: an internal screen we designed to watch our own data pipeline. It followed each trip step by step (from the Geotab device, into the backend, through scoring, to the result on the dashboard) and showed where a trip went missing or arrived late. So when a score looked wrong or slow, we could see exactly which step broke instead of guessing.

Bentley Mulliner is the bespoke arm of Bentley Motors. Customers don't pick from a catalogue; they specify a car. The existing iOS app, built to showcase the brand, didn't serve that decision: it described vehicles instead of helping anyone configure one. I led the redesign from a static reference app into a real-time decision tool. Customers and Bentley executives could now build a complete specification, see it rendered immediately, and pass the result to a dealership for pricing. The work covered UX strategy, information architecture, high-fidelity design, and a rendering technique developed with engineering that gave us photoreal output without 3D, a constraint that ended up defining the product. After launch, the app became the default surface for in-showroom configuration. Dealer follow-ups became structured rather than improvised: every build left the room as the same structured summary, ready for pricing.

For a Bentley buyer specifying a Mulliner build, the configuration moment is the most important decision of the purchase. Spec choices shift the price by significant amounts, and once committed, materials enter a production pipeline that takes months to reverse. The cost of a wrong call is high, both for the customer and for Bentley. The original app was built to communicate craftsmanship, not to support that decision. It showed renderings of completed cars and reference imagery of trim options, but customers had no way to see their own combination. Reaching confidence required either imagination, picturing a colour from a swatch and a stitching pattern from a flat image and combining them mentally, or a multi-stop dealer conversation that often stretched across weeks.

What was broken. Dealerships were never under-equipped: physical swatches, material samples, and reference vehicles were all on the floor. What no showroom could offer was the customer's own combination, assembled: this colour on this body with this interior and this stitching. That composed view lived only in the customer's imagination, and confidence built slowly because of it. The digital experience, meanwhile, showed finished reference cars, it communicated the craft without supporting the decision in progress.

Design challenge. How might we let a customer specify a bespoke Bentley in real time, with enough visual confidence to commit, while staying within the performance ceiling of an iPad in a showroom? The product moved from being a brochure to being part of the sales process.

p.u: Customers don't know what they want until they see it
p.x: Customers don't know what they want until they see it. A Mulliner spec involves combinations of finishes most people have never seen together. Showing a swatch and a description is not the same as showing the car. The product had to render every choice immediately and unconditionally, no apply button, no preview state, no waiting. How we knew Bentley’s own data on real buyers, brought to us as the problem statement, and the stakeholder sessions that unpacked it: swatches, samples and reference cars were on every showroom floor, and buyers still could not picture their own combination, confidence built over weeks of visits. → Decision 1 Read from Bentley’s buyer data · the stakeholder sessions that unpacked it 02

p.u: Letting customers roam freely didn't help them
p.x: Letting customers roam freely didn't help them. The first prototype let users jump between any option in any order. In review, this didn't help anyone: customers got lost, and advisors had to step in to guide. Constraining the experience into a sequence (model → exterior → interior → wheels → personalisation → review) was one of the more important calls in the project, and not the obvious one. How we knew The first prototype was free-form. Reviewed with Bentley’s stakeholders against what their buyer data showed, customers get lost without structure and advisors end up coaching, it was replaced by the guided sequence. → Decision 2 Read from the first prototype, reviewed against the buyer data 03

p.u: The real output is the build summary, not the screen
p.x: The real output is the build summary, not the screen. What sales advisors valued most wasn't the configurator itself, it was what came out of it: a clean build summary they could hand to the dealership and production team without any translation or rework. The screens exist to produce that document. Once we understood this, sharing stopped being an export feature buried in a menu and became a core surface of the product. How we knew Workflow reviews with Bentley’s stakeholders and Mulliner-trained advisors: what mattered downstream was a build summary the dealership and production team could use without translation or rework. → Decision 3 Read from workflow reviews with Mulliner-trained advisors

p.s: 06 The constraint that became the technique
p.x: The decision that defined the product came first and was technical: there would be no 3D. It gets its own section because everything after it depends on it.

p.s: 06 The constraint that became the technique
p.x: Decision 1: Real-time visual feedback without 3D. Before The brief assumed real-time 3D. At Bentley fidelity on showroom iPads that meant loading waits or visible quality loss, and Bentley accepts neither. After Every option a flat PNG layer at a fixed position; colour as a fill under a 0.8-opacity detail layer. One body set wears every colour, and choices render at once, on older iPads too. The original brief assumed a 3D rendering pipeline. After evaluating options, the team concluded that real-time 3D was not viable at the visual fidelity Bentley required. Load times would have broken the experience; reducing fidelity would have broken the brand. Instead of dropping fidelity, we changed the technique: Every customisable component (body, wheels, interior panels, stitching, trim inlays) rendered as a flat PNG layer at a fixed dimension, with pixel-accurate X/Y positioning derived from a master Photoshop layout

p.s: 06 The constraint that became the technique
p.x: Colour works through layering, not asset swaps: the body's detail layer (all the lighting, reflections, and shading) sits at roughly 0.8 opacity over a flat colour fill, so any paint colour shows through while the surface detail stays intact One set of body assets wears every colour in the range The result felt indistinguishable from a render, loaded immediately, and held up on older iPads. Tradeoff: the asset production pipeline was heavier than 3D would have required. Each new model meant a new layered Photoshop file, with every option matted out at a consistent vanishing point, across the project this came to more than 1,500 PNG assets, produced and positioned by hand. We absorbed that cost in the design team because it was a one-time investment per model and a permanent gain in runtime quality. One greyscale detail layer (lighting, reflections, shading) at 0.8 opacity over a flat colour. Change the colour; the detail never changes. Slide the opacity to see why 0.8 was the number.
With choose-and-see solved, the remaining decisions shaped the experience around it. Each is told as before and after.

p.u: Decision 2: A guided sequence, not free exploration
p.x: Decision 2: A guided sequence, not free exploration. Before Free exploration in any order, the first prototype. Customers wandered instead of committing, and advisors ended up coaching. After Model, exterior, interior, wheels, personalisation, review. Step back any time, never skip ahead; advisors step in at predictable moments. Free-form configuration was the obvious default, and the one we built first. Review with Bentley’s stakeholders, against what their own buyer data showed, made the case for replacing it: customers who can touch anything spend more time wandering than committing, and the lack of structure pushes advisors into a coaching role they aren’t in the room to perform. The guided flow (model → exterior → interior → wheels → personalisation → review) gave the experience a rhythm and let advisors step in at predictable moments. We kept the ability to step back through earlier decisions, but removed the ability to skip ahead. The customer always saw the next decision and never lost their place.

p.u: Decision 3: Share as a first-class action
p.x: Decision 3: Share as a first-class action. Before Sharing as an export, tucked in a menu at the end of the flow. After The primary action of the Review screen: one tap sends a structured summary to the dealer, in the format the build team consumes directly. Sharing isn't a flourish at the end of the flow; it's the point. The Review screen is where the configurator earns its keep. A finished build generates a structured summary that goes to the dealer as a single tap, in a format the build team can consume directly. This decision changed the information architecture. Sharing isn't tucked under a menu; it's the primary action of the final screen, and it's why the product exists.

Decision 4: Builds persist across sessions. Before A build lived for one visit, while a Mulliner sale spans several. After A lightweight account and a build history the advisor pulls up at the next meeting, with every choice intact, on the same device or another. A Mulliner sale spans multiple visits. Builds had to survive between sessions, on the same device or another one. We added a lightweight account model and a build history that an advisor could pull up at the start of the next meeting, with full version state intact.

p.u: The screen’s contract and the architecture
p.x: The screen’s contract and the architecture.

Information architecture. Home → Browse models → Select model → Visualizer (Exterior → Interior → Wheels → Personalisation) → Review → Share The visualizer sits at the centre of the product. Every other screen either gets the customer there or handles the artefact it produces.

Interaction principles. The car is always visible. No control covers more than roughly a third of the screen at any time. Choices commit on tap; there is no apply button. Material and colour previews use a single lighting setup so customers can trust the consistency of what they see across selections. We worked within Bentley's brand guidelines, which kept the primary action identical on every screen, customers always know where the next step is.

Constraints we worked within. The asset pipeline meant each new model required lead time on Photoshop layering. The information architecture was built to accommodate this, new models slot into the existing category structure without redesign. Showroom connectivity is unreliable. The configurator works offline by default; sharing falls back gracefully when it can't reach a network.

The most valuable part of a luxury digital product is what isn’t on screen. What came out, and what each removal gave back. Real-time 3D Replaced by layered PNGs: the fidelity stayed and the loading went. Free-form navigation Replaced by a five-step sequence: customers stopped wandering, advisors stopped coaching. The apply button and the preview state Every choice commits on tap and renders immediately. No gap between choose and see. The swatch-only state No option is shown as a swatch on its own; every choice is shown on the customer’s car. Share, buried in a menu It became the primary action of the final screen. Small buttons and controls Interactions rebuilt around tap and scroll, the two gestures nobody gets wrong. Nested screens The navigation hierarchy was flattened after walkthroughs showed people backing out of them. Public availability (later, Bentley’s call) Open access let anyone send casual build requests to dealers. Restricted to executive and showroom use, it went back to serious buyers.

p.s: 10 What changed, and what I can’t claim
p.x: The hardest interface problem was fitting the customisation controls onto a compact mobile screen. The option selectors ran edge to edge, and on a small display the early versions felt cramped and fiddly to operate accessibly. We stripped out buttons and small controls wherever possible and rebuilt the interactions around tap and scroll, the two gestures nobody gets wrong. That's why the shipped product has so few visible controls. Navigation hierarchy was simplified after early walkthroughs showed people backing out of nested screens. Visual hierarchy on the review screen was rebuilt to make the share action unmistakable; it had originally been buried as a secondary button. Aligning the layered PNG assets was unforgiving work. Every layer had to sit in exactly the right position, a deviation of even one pixel put a wheel or a trim line visibly out of place and broke the illusion of a single render. Getting each asset set to register perfectly took repeated adjustment rounds between design and engineering.

p.s: 10 What changed, and what I can’t claim
p.x: What changed in practice. The configurator became the default surface for in-showroom Mulliner conversations. The iPad sat between customer and advisor as the shared surface for composing the complete build, working alongside the physical samples on the floor, not replacing them. Submissions to the build team became uniform. Every build left the room as the same structured summary (the same option codes, the same ordering) which meant less verification work for the production team downstream. Customers left sessions with a build they had specified themselves rather than a build the advisor had narrated to them. The qualitative shift that mattered most was the decline in requests to physically see a reference car before committing, the configurator was the reference.

p.s: 10 What changed, and what I can’t claim
p.x: Bentley later pulled the app from public availability, for a practical reason: open access meant anyone could send a build request to a dealership, and many of those requests were casual, sent on a whim, with no response when dealers followed up. Restricting the app to executives and showroom use put it back in the hands of serious buyers, in the room where builds are actually specified. It had a second benefit: on showroom iPads, the compact-mobile-screen problem stopped mattering, the interface had the space it worked best at. The move cut off any public-facing metrics, but the product was retained exactly where it earned its keep.

p.s: 10 What changed, and what I can’t claim
p.u: Honest limits on what I can claim
p.x: Honest limits on what I can claim. This was an agency engagement, which means I don't have access to post-launch telemetry from Bentley's side. I can speak to the qualitative shifts I observed in stakeholder reviews, advisor workflow reviews and our own walkthroughs; I can't claim a specific completion-rate lift or transaction-time reduction. The numbers I would want (sessions per build, share-to-pricing time, build-to-order conversion) sit on Bentley's side and weren't part of the contractual scope. A portfolio piece is more useful when it's honest about this than when it borrows credibility from numbers nobody can verify.

p.s: 10 What changed, and what I can’t claim
p.x: Learnings I've taken forward. Real-time visual feedback is the most important single factor in a high-value configurator. Every other usability improvement I made on this project, combined, was smaller than the gain from removing the gap between choose and see. A performance constraint can become a design technique. The layered-PNG system started as a workaround for an absent 3D pipeline; it ended as a faster, sharper rendering approach than 3D would have given us at this fidelity. The most valuable part of a luxury digital product is what isn't on screen. Everything we removed (the free-form navigation, the apply button, the swatch-only state, the menu-buried share) contributed more to the experience than anything we added.

Market research has always traded depth for scale. Sagan refuses the trade: it's an AI interviewer, it speaks, listens, probes, and follows up, holding a real research conversation with physicians and patients at whatever scale a study needs. ZoomRx has been AI-first from the start; Sagan is that conviction applied to the interview itself. I designed the interview experience across web and mobile: the conversation and its turn-taking, the captioning system, the switches between spoken and on-screen answers, and the recovery paths for an audience that gets interrupted for a living. Submission rates and participation increased by ~30% versus text-based formats, measured before and after deployment, and within the year Sagan was a product ZoomRx sells to pharma companies.

Market research offers two bad options. A qualitative interview delivers depth, but needs a trained human moderator, a scheduled call, and budgets that keep samples small. A survey delivers scale, but flattens open answers into typed fragments from respondents racing to finish. The depth-versus-scale tradeoff is structural, and physician time makes it worse: the people whose answers matter most have the least patience for either format. Because ZoomRx designs the studies itself (the drafts, the paths, the logic) an AI could credibly hold the moderator's chair: the conversation probes freely inside a structure we already know.
Design challenge. How might we make an interview with an AI feel like talking to a good human moderator, for a professional audience with zero patience for friction?

p.u: A conversation needs a visible turn-taker
p.x: A conversation needs a visible turn-taker. When someone speaks to a machine, the twin anxieties are "did it hear me?" and "should I be talking now?" Every state (listening, processing, moderator speaking) had to be explicit, or respondents talk over the AI, repeat themselves, and trust collapses. How we knew Internal UAT: the design and development team and the community team ran the interview end to end, repeatedly. Without explicit states, testers talked over the moderator, repeated themselves, or sat waiting for nothing. → Decision 2 Read from internal UAT, end to end, repeatedly 02

p.u: The screen remembers what sound can't
p.x: The screen remembers what sound can't. Spoken words disappear the moment they're said. So the screen keeps the record: captions while the AI talks, and a history of every answer already given. If you missed something or want to check something, it's there. How we knew The same UAT rounds, run audio-only first: a missed question had no way back, and in an interview a missed question is a broken answer. Captions followed, then the wall-of-text problem, then the eight-word cap and the history view. → Decisions 3 and 5 Read from UAT rounds run audio-only first 03

p.u: Some questions need to be seen, not heard
p.x: Some questions need to be seen, not heard. Talking is the richest way to answer "why." But when a question involves something to look at (an ad, a reference image, a set of options to compare) voice alone fails: you can't speak a picture. Those moments move to the screen, and the design had to know which was which, question by question. How we knew ZoomRx’s own study designs: stimulus questions (an ad, a reference image, options to compare) already existed in the studies Sagan would run, and none of them can be spoken. → Decision 4 Read from ZoomRx’s own study designs
Each decision answers one moment where a conversation with a machine breaks.

p.u: Decision 1: An interviewer, not a form with a voice
p.x: Decision 1: An interviewer, not a form with a voice. The moment A respondent gives an interesting answer. A form with a voice would simply read out the next question. The response Sagan probes like a good moderator, bounded by the study structure ZoomRx designed, so it digs in without drifting off-study. Sagan doesn't read a questionnaire aloud, it runs the interview. It introduces itself, asks, listens, and probes with follow-ups the way a good moderator digs into an interesting answer. We could let it do that safely because we design the studies ourselves: the AI probes freely inside a structure whose every path we already know. Tradeoff: an AI that probes can drift off-study. Bounding it to the research structure gave up some spontaneity, and bought the reliability a recorded medical-adjacent conversation cannot do without.

p.u: Decision 2: Whose turn it is, always visible
p.x: Decision 2: Whose turn it is, always visible. The moment The respondent stops talking and nothing happens. Did it hear me? Should I speak? Is it broken? The response Every state is named on screen (preparing, connecting, setting up audio, listening, processing) with a persistent indicator of who holds the floor. A voice conversation fails the moment nobody knows whose turn it is. Every state is explicit: Preparing your interview room. Connecting your moderator. Setting up audio. Listening… Processing your response…, with a persistent indicator showing whether the moderator or you holds the floor. Even the pre-interview sequence is deliberate ritual: it frames what follows as a meeting, not a form. Tradeoff: more visible machinery than a minimal aesthetic would want. Accepted: in voice, reassurance beats minimalism. PREPARING YOUR INTERVIEW ROOM Setting up a quiet room for you. MODERATOR YOU Every state is explicit, and every caption is eight words or fewer. Step through the sequence a respondent actually sees.

p.u: Decision 3: Captions, capped at eight words
p.x: Decision 3: Captions, capped at eight words. The moment The moderator asks something long and the respondent catches half of it. In an interview, a missed question is a broken answer. The response Everything Sagan says is captioned, eight words at a time; the respondent’s own speech is never captioned. Everything Sagan says is captioned on screen, and each caption holds a maximum of eight words, so the text stays big enough to read at a glance. Nothing gets missed, with or without sound. Tradeoff: the cap constrains the writing itself, every question has to be phrased for the ear and for an eight-word screen. Harder to write, easier to follow.

p.u: Decision 4: Voice where it's rich, screen where it's precise
p.x: Decision 4: Voice where it's rich, screen where it's precise. The moment The question is about an ad, a reference image or a 1–6 rating. You cannot speak a picture. The response The conversation switches to the screen: a tap for a rating, the image for a stimulus, a checklist with typed input for a multi-select. Open-ended answers are spoken. But a 1–6 rating is a tap, a stimulus is an image on screen, and a multi-select is a checklist with typed input where the options don't fit. The conversation switches modality to whatever makes the answer most accurate. V2 added the single-select beside them, and kept every option speakable: say it instead of tapping it and the answer is mapped to the nearest option on screen, mispronounced or not. Tradeoff: switching between speaking and tapping mid-conversation risks breaking the flow, the turn-taking states exist partly to make those hand-offs feel natural.

p.u: Decision 5: The interview survives real life
p.x: Decision 5: The interview survives real life. The moment A patient walks in mid-interview. A linear interview would punish exactly the busy respondents the research wants most. The response Sagan notices the silence, asks “Are you there?”, offers a break and saves progress; on return it recaps before continuing. Clinicians get interrupted. Sagan notices silence ("Are you there?"), offers breaks, saves progress, and when the respondent returns, it recaps what was already discussed before continuing. The interview ends properly too: completion, the honorarium payment initiated, and a transcript-style history the respondent can revisit. The panel card carries the way back too: the time remaining and Continue interview, so a paused interview is never lost in the dashboard. Tradeoff: an interruptible interview is more work to design than a linear one. But an interview that punishes interruption would select against exactly the busy, senior respondents the research wants most.

p.u: The thread that ran through them
p.x: The thread that ran through them. Two problems were the hardest, and both came from the same place: in an AI interview, the user gets lost easily. The first: whose turn is it? Every version was tested end to end in UAT, the design and development team and the community team, round after round, before any physician saw it. In early versions, testers couldn't tell when the AI was speaking, when it was their turn, or why there was silence while the AI prepared a follow-up. Every one of those gaps broke the conversation: people talked over the moderator, repeated themselves, or sat waiting for nothing. Defining the full set of states (moderator speaking, listening, processing, preparing the next question) was the most complicated design work in the product, precisely because human conversation makes turn-taking invisible and an AI conversation has to make it explicit. The second: how much should the screen say while the AI speaks?

p.u: The thread that ran through them
p.x: We started audio-only: the purest version of a conversation. It had a real flaw: if a respondent misses something the AI said, there's no way to recover it, and in an interview, a missed question is a broken answer. So we added closed captions. But a wall of text pulls attention away from listening and quietly turns the conversation back into reading. The answer was YouTube-style captioning: short lines, a maximum of eight words at a time: big, glanceable, gone. Enough to catch what you missed, never enough to compete with the voice. And for anything beyond the moment, the history state: recall any answer already given, so nothing depends on memory. That sequence, audio-only → captions → capped captions + history, is the product's learning, in shipped form. And the two threads together, the turn-taking states and the caption system, are why the interview feels effortless: the hardest work in the product is the machinery you barely notice.

The interview, end to end. Profile verification → the study card with its honorarium → guidance (find a quiet spot; don't share personally identifying information) → the room-preparation sequence → the conversation → completion, payment initiated, dashboard. One arc, identical across web and mobile, the interview is the product on both.
The history state. A transcript-style view lets respondents recall every answer they've given. The conversation is never a black box, and stepping away never means losing your place.

The timing is the point. This was built in the early ChatGPT era, when nothing was settled, how an AI answer should look, how sources should show, what happens when a question is too big. p.s: 02 An answer nobody knew how to draw
p.x: Life-sciences teams sit on enormous, fragmented information: trial results, competitive moves, regulatory events, conference intelligence. Getting an answer meant knowing which source held it and having the time to dig. Generic large language models offered speed but failed the domain: a confident answer with a wrong drug name is worse than a slow answer. And underneath that sat the design problem with no borrowed solution: nobody knew what an AI answer to a clinical question should look like. Not how long, not how structured, not how sourced, not what to do when the question returns three thousand results. The interface conventions didn't exist. We had to design them.

p.s: 02 An answer nobody knew how to draw
p.x: Design challenge. How should an AI answer a question when the person asking is paid to be right, and no design conventions exist yet?

p.s: 03 Who asks, and what they need
p.x: Four teams ask, and every one of them is paid to be right. Roles, not invented people, and the jobs each one needed the product to do. THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO CI analyst When I ask a clinical question, I want the answer to show where it came from, so I can quote it in a client report. BD&L analyst When I compare trials or assets, I want them side by side with sources attached, so comparison is an operation, not copy-and-paste. Any analyst When my question is too vague or too big, I want help shaping it, so I don’t get three thousand results, or nothing. Any analyst When research spans days, I want my findings to accumulate, so I’m not pasting answers into documents to keep them. Team When a colleague has done the work, we want to share it with the right permissions, so AI research becomes a team asset. Requirements came from the problems analysts hit using it, and, for the workspace, from the document I wrote proposing what Ferma should become.

p.s: 05 What the first analysts taught us
p.u: Expert users don't want answers; they want defensible answers
p.x: Expert users don't want answers; they want defensible answers. An analyst quotes Ferma's output in reports read by clients. Every response needed a visible chain back to evidence: the interface had to support verification as a first-class behaviour, not a footnote. How we knew ZoomRx’s own analysts, who quote answers in client reports, and the benchmark against ChatGPT and Perplexity: a confident generic answer with a wrong drug name is worse than a slow one. → Calls 1 and 2 Read from in-house analysts and the ChatGPT / Perplexity benchmark 02

p.s: 05 What the first analysts taught us
p.u: Asking is easy in chat; research isn't
p.x: Asking is easy in chat; research isn't. A chat flow answers one question at a time. Real research is non-linear: analysts follow several paths, abandon some, come back to old insights and connect them. Constrained to chat alone, they were manually copying pieces of answers into documents to use later. The product had to become a place where research accumulates, not just a place where questions get answered. How we knew Working alongside the in-house analysts: constrained to chat, they were copying pieces of answers into documents to use later, the behaviour that argued for a workspace. → Call 5 Read from working alongside the in-house analysts 03

p.s: 05 What the first analysts taught us
p.u: The question itself is a design problem
p.x: The question itself is a design problem. An empty search bar is intimidating when the question isn't framed yet, and a badly scoped question returns three thousand results nobody can use. The design had to help on both ends: suggesting what to ask before typing, and helping narrow the ask when it came back too big. How we knew An empty search bar when the question isn’t framed yet, and three thousand results when it is too broad, both seen with the first analysts using it. → Call 3 Read from the first analysts using it

Every chatbot of the time streamed prose. For a clinical question that is the wrong object: nobody can scan it, and nobody can defend it. So the answer became something designed, with an anatomy per kind of ask and the same things on every one of them: citation chips, the sources panel, feedback and copy.
No patterns existed to borrow, so the decisions were made on the boards, with the options they beat drawn beside them. Five calls, as logged.

p.u: Call 1: The answer is a designed object, not generated text
p.x: Call 1: The answer is a designed object, not generated text. CALL 01 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD How should an AI answer to a clinical question look? On the table, not taken The call Instead, every answer type got a designed anatomy. Structured summaries with named fields (Efficacy, Safety, Drug, Indications) where the ask was specific; narrative layouts with a strict typographic hierarchy where it was open-ended; long answers split into short points with a background summary up top and drug names bolded; multi-result answers as collapsed cards, with the truncation call recorded on the board at the moment it was made: show the collapsed view, one field visible. Tradeoff: every format is a template, and a template can mis-fit an answer. We carried formats per ask-type plus a narrative fallback, more design surface to maintain, in exchange for answers an analyst can scan in seconds and defend in a meeting.

p.u: Call 2: Evidence lives inside the answer
p.x: Call 2: Evidence lives inside the answer. CALL 02 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD Where do the sources live? On the table, not taken The call THE PANEL ITSELF: FOUR LAYOUTS, COMPARED SIDE BY SIDE BEFORE CHOOSING Sources are part of the response, not an appendix: citation chips on every claim-carrying block, and a sources panel, fifty references deep when it had to be, with search built in. We explored the panel's form deliberately: paginated at five, at ten, scrolling, scrolling-plus-pagination, laid side by side and compared before choosing. The design bet underneath it all: for this audience, verifiability is usability. Tradeoff: denser responses and slower reading than a clean chat bubble. Accepted: the audience is paid to verify.

p.u: Call 3: When the question is too big or too vague, the AI helps shape it
p.x: Call 3: When the question is too big or too vague, the AI helps shape it. CALL 03 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD What happens when a question is too big, or not framed yet? On the table, not taken The call Broad questions got a designed response of their own: the AI explains the scope problem and offers tailored ways to narrow (by category, time period, specific study, demographic, outcome) written as help, with concrete example questions. And before any question is typed, the empty state suggests what's worth asking, because a blank box is a wall when the question isn't framed yet. Tradeoff: declining to answer risks feeling unhelpful. The nudges had to read as "here's how to get what you actually want", a copywriting and tone problem as much as an interface one, with response templates written and rewritten for exactly that.

p.u: Call 3: When the question is too big or too vague, the AI helps shape it
p.x: The same idea, scoping the question before it is answered, grew into focus areas. A focus area holds the firms, drugs, indications, drug classes, targets and development stages a team cares about, and refines every conversation until it is switched; switching starts a new chat, so answers never mix two scopes.

p.u: Call 4: Comparison as a first-class operation
p.x: Call 4: Comparison as a first-class operation. CALL 04 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD How do two trials get compared? On the table, not taken The call AND ITS FIRST ITERATION, FROM THE ANALYSTS USING IT Before After Analysts compare things for a living, trials, drugs, readouts. So comparison isn't a paragraph; it's a table: named rows (Phase, Enrollment, Arms, Efficacy, Safety, Conclusion), two entities side by side, sources attached. And the table earned its own iteration from real feedback: expanding truncated cells one by one was too many clicks, so we added Expand Content to open them all at once, and renamed the old Expand to Fullscreen so the two couldn't be confused. Tradeoff: tables inside a conversation break the chat metaphor. Accepted without hesitation: the metaphor serves the analyst, not the other way round.

p.u: Call 5: Beyond the chat: research as the container
p.x: Call 5: Beyond the chat: research as the container. CALL 05 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD What container does research need? On the table, not taken The call As the product matured, I wrote the argument that the chat paradigm itself was the ceiling, a document proposing what Ferma should become: workflows and tasks as the core concept, with agent selection removed as a user burden (an orchestrator routes to agents invisibly); profiles (business development, competitive intelligence, scientific communications, new product planning) each carrying pre-built key tasks; and spaces where highlighted responses, insights, and charts accumulate per goal, get compared and tracked, and turn into shareable reports. Chat remains how you ask; the workspace is where research lives. Tradeoff: proposing a structural change is slower and riskier than shipping the next feature, it has to convince people before it can exist. That's why it was written down, with the flows designed alongside the argument.

The board kept the score. The design boards are themselves the validation record, decisions were made in public, on the canvas, with their reasoning attached: Options explored side by side before choosing, the sources panel's four layout variants, the summary truncation alternatives Decisions written where they were made: "DECISION: show the collapsed view, one field truncated" sits on the board next to the options it beat Iterations traceable to feedback: Expand Content exists because the analysts using it said expanding cells one by one was too many clicks; the old button was renamed Fullscreen in the same stroke A feedback loop shipped in the product: every response carries its own feedback control, so the answer formats kept learning from the people using them
Call 5 was not a feature. It was an argument that the container was wrong, written down because it had to convince people before it could exist. Here it is drawn.

p.u: Sharing AI work, before anyone had a pattern for it
p.x: Sharing AI work, before anyone had a pattern for it. Research that accumulates is research a team wants to share. Explorer and Viewer roles, team-gated access, a library of shared chats, and sharing to the team kept apart from sharing in public: collaboration patterns for AI conversations, designed while the conversations themselves were still new.

Designing where no patterns existed. This is the section other case studies can't have, because the work happened before the conventions did. Packaging a design system as an agent skill, then building the pipeline that uses it: a survey draft in, reviewed on-brand screens out, graded against a rubric before a human ever sees them. IN 10 SECONDS PROBLEM Every survey needs the same instructional screens designed again, by hand, at a quality no one could hold steady. EVIDENCE Fourteen real survey drafts parsed by the pipeline itself, four working sessions with the design lead, and the output format checked by pasting it into the live survey platform. BUILT A design system as a machine-readable skill, a corpus-derived screen taxonomy, and an orchestrated designer–evaluator loop with human gates. STATUS In use. The SPI team, who build the surveys, now turn a draft into reviewed boilerplate screens in about an hour; it used to take three teams around seven days.

MY ROLE Senior Product Designer, ZoomRx, I own the design side: the design system skill, the screen taxonomy, the emphasis rule and the evaluator's rubric. Architecture and review with a design-leadership partner; the pipeline itself is Claude Code plugins and sub-agents I specced and dog-fooded. The design question underneath: what has to exist before a machine can produce work a designer would sign off on? Role Senior Product Designer, ZoomRx: design system, taxonomy, rubric, pipeline spec Platform Claude Code plugin: skills, sub-agents, an MCP asset server Status In use by the SPI team; eight canonical screens frozen, design and token skills derived from them; dog-fooded over 14 real drafts Team Me on the design side, with a design-leadership partner on architecture and review ~100 questions in a survey draft · 67 in-scope boilerplates across 14 drafts · 5 compositional archetypes → ~8 canonical screens · 3 sub-agents, one rubric, two human gates Most of this case study is a judgement call about where design belongs in an automated pipeline, and one reversal I had to accept.

67 in-scope boilerplates, pulled from 14 real survey drafts by the pipeline’s own parsing step 76% of them are Statements: one short paragraph on a card. Get that screen right and most output is right ~1 hr from a survey draft to reviewed boilerplate screens, by the SPI team alone. It used to take three teams around seven days

A ZoomRx survey draft arrives as a Word document of roughly a hundred questions. Between those questions sit the boilerplates: the instructional, orienting and transition screens that tell a physician what is about to happen. They are not questions, they carry no data, and they get designed by hand for every study, which means they are the first thing to slip when a team is busy. Getting them built took three teams and around seven days per survey. I built two things. First, the ZoomRx MR design system packaged as a skill: tokens, components, icons and golden structures written so a model can compose a screen without guessing values. Then the Boilerplate Generator, a plugin that reads a draft, decides which boilerplates are worth designing, drafts each one, and has a second agent grade it against a rubric until it clears a bar, with a human gating both the selection and the final output. A design system expressed as primitive → semantic → component tokens, because semantic naming is what makes a system legible to a model

A screen taxonomy derived from the real corpus, not from intuition A designer–evaluator loop deliberately made adversarial A rubric where fidelity and emphasis are pass/fail, not matters of taste The result: the SPI team, the team that builds the surveys, now does it alone, in about an hour. The version before this one worked and was still wrong: one context window did everything, so long runs blew the window and the model started emitting nonsense. A run took around 30 minutes and ~110k tokens for 7–10 boilerplates, the sub-agents were improvised at runtime so behaviour drifted between runs, and the evaluator accepted work with "only trivial nitpicks", a judgement call dressed as a standard. We restarted from a clean slate, carrying the design intent and nothing else.

Boilerplates are the easiest screens in the product and the most repeated. Hand-designing them does not scale, but automating them naively produces the thing every designer fears: output that is technically on-brand and visibly wrong, an illustration forced onto a one-sentence screen, a drug name shouting in a pill, a paragraph quietly reworded by a model that thought it could write better than the regulator-approved source. The real opportunity was not speed. It was the quality floor: if the system can hold a bar without a designer in the loop for every screen, then the designer's time moves to the screens that deserve it.
Design challenge. How might a pipeline produce screens a designer would sign off on, when no designer will look at most of them?

Four people stand around every generated screen, and only one of them is a designer. THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO Product designer When a study needs forty boilerplate screens, I want them generated to the bar I’d sign off, so my time goes to the screens that deserve it. Reviewing designer When the output is wrong, I want to say so in plain language and have the pipeline try again, so review is a conversation, not a rebuild. Study author When a boilerplate is regulator-approved copy, I want it reproduced exactly, so no model rewords it. Research ops When a draft comes in, I want to confirm scope before anything is designed, so the cheapest error is caught first.
