p.s: 05 What the first versions taught us
p.u: A model can't use a design system it has to interpret
p.x: A model can't use a design system it has to interpret. The first version derived its visual rules from the legacy codebase and from the draft text. That produced values without meaning. The fix was to build the design system as a skill first: three token tiers where the semantic layer carries the role (text.primary, surface.canvas, button.primary) rather than the value, so an agent picks tokens by intent instead of copying hexes. The same repository holds the icon library, the illustrations and golden structures, so an agent composing a screen has the real inventory rather than a description of it. How we knew Reviewing V1 output: values derived from the legacy codebase and the draft text carried no meaning, so the agent copied hexes instead of choosing by intent. → the skill’s three token tiers Read from reviewing V1 output 02

p.s: 05 What the first versions taught us
p.u: Design has to come from a canvas, not from a paragraph
p.x: Design has to come from a canvas, not from a paragraph. This is the lesson I most had to be argued into. I kept deriving design from the source text: read the boilerplates, infer the patterns, write the token set, and let the screens follow. My design-leadership partner's position was the opposite, design the screens on a canvas first, react to them, and derive the rule set afterwards. He was right. The text-derived layer asserted visual opinions ("one white card") that nobody had designed or reacted to, and was internally inconsistent, it cited three different boilerplate counts in three sections of the same document. We retired it and rebuilt top-down. How we knew A design-leadership partner’s critique across four working sessions, logged as it was raised: the text-derived layer asserted visual opinions nobody had designed and contradicted itself on boilerplate counts. Retired, rebuilt top-down from eight screens designed on the canvas. → The two reversals Read from four working sessions with the design lead 03

p.s: 05 What the first versions taught us
p.u: An evaluator that shares the designer's criteria will rubber-stamp it
p.x: An evaluator that shares the designer's criteria will rubber-stamp it. The first loop had the designer and the evaluator grading by the same criteria on the same model, which is not a review: it is a model approving its own reasoning. Divergence had to be designed in deliberately, a different model, criteria the designer is never told to optimise for, and a scorecard rather than a verdict. How we knew The first loop’s results: a designer and an evaluator grading on the same criteria, on the same model, approved each other’s work, “only trivial nitpicks”. → Decisions 2 and 3 Read from the first loop’s results

p.s: 06 Two reversals before the first screen
p.x: Four revisions and two reversals came before the first screen was designed. Both reversals were mine to accept, and both taught the same thing from different directions: the rules come after the design, never before it. REV 1 An architecture reset Three agents, not four: I proposed folding brief writing into the classifier, and the extra agent was dropped. One overall brief per study plus a thin brief per boilerplate; audience came out of the briefs because the copy and the design never change with it. REV 2 The architecture as files The agreed design turned into real agent and skill files: three sub-agents and five skills, each declared once. REV 3 · REVERSAL Design derived from text I wrote the orchestrator and parsing skills for real, then derived a token set and a pattern document from the legacy codebase and the draft text. It asserted “one white card” that nobody had designed or reacted to, and cited three different boilerplate counts in three sections.

p.s: 06 Two reversals before the first screen
p.x: WHAT IT TAUGHT Retired. A rule written from text is an opinion nobody has looked at. Design has to be reacted to on a canvas first. REV 4 The corpus The parsing step, run over 14 real drafts, pulled out 67 in-scope boilerplates with their verbatim text. Classified from first principles, they reduced to eight canonical screens. FIRST PASS · REVERSAL AI renders of the eight I generated the eight in three AI design tools as a starting point. The review was blunt: “We are skipping over the most important part, which is the expression of your design judgment.” The renders had no real content either. WHAT IT TAUGHT Sent back. Design all eight by hand, on one canvas, with real copy from the corpus and the product’s own colours. THE CANVAS Eight screens, designed and frozen Designed with real boilerplate text, reviewed, then frozen as the source of truth: the target the designer agent aims at and the standard the evaluator grades against. DERIVED Then the rules

p.s: 06 Two reversals before the first screen
p.x: Primitive tokens exported from the frozen file; the semantic layer, the composition skill and the emphasis rendering derived from the screens; a V0 rubric; and the output format checked against the live survey platform. Dog-fooding was the useful move: the parsing skill had to work well enough to produce the corpus that the design layer is built on, so the pipeline validated one of its own parts before anything downstream existed.

These eight are the golden reference for everything the pipeline produces. They are bundled inside the design skill, so the designer agent composes toward them and the evaluator grades against the same eight. Everything else in the project, the tokens, the composition rules, the emphasis rendering and the rubric, is derived from them. Each carries its share of the 67 boilerplates in the corpus.

p.u: Why eight, and why these eight
p.x: Why eight, and why these eight. Rather than guess which layouts were needed, I ran the parsing step across 14 real drafts to pull out 67 in-scope boilerplates with their verbatim text, then classified that corpus from first principles. It collapsed into five compositional archetypes (Statement, Structured List, Asset Hand-off, Composite, Comparison Matrix) and the distribution settled the priorities: 76% are Statements, a single short paragraph on a card. Get that one screen right and three-quarters of all output is right. Functional intent (inform, instruct, prepare, orient, transition) does not drive layout, so it became a second axis that tunes tone, emphasis and whether an illustration is allowed at all. Density became a third. Five archetypes across those axes reduce to roughly eight canonical screens and a component inventory of about fifteen blocks.

Illustration only where it orients. Illustrations come from ZoomRx’s own brand-asset library, reached through an MCP server: the designer agent searches it, picks an asset and references it by its address, and it is the only agent given that connection, so the evaluator judges the choice without having made it. The rule is strict and ordered: an illustration if one genuinely fits, otherwise an icon, otherwise nothing; never a decorative “close enough”. Only screens that orient or prepare may carry one, centred above the text; definitions, transitions and dense screens stand on typography. The evaluator scores an off-topic image as a zero.

Here is one screen followed all the way down: what was designed, the semantic tokens it became, and the HTML the designer agent has to emit for the survey platform to accept it. 1 · ON THE CANVAS 2 · IN THE TOKEN LIBRARY Heading type-title · 26 / 34 · medium · #132D52 Lead-in type-body · 18 / 26 · regular · #4E4E4E Definition row surface-muted · radius 8 · #F6F7F8 Term label · navy, gloss in gray · #132D52 Divider border-divider · 1px · #EDEDED The card surface-card · radius 10 · padding 40 · #FFFFFF 3 · IN THE PASTE FORMAT Why the third column looks like that. Pasted into the live survey platform, the HTML field kept nothing but inline styles: no style block, no variables, no media queries, no head or body. So the designer agent reasons in semantic tokens and writes their literal values inline, and the rubric scores any style block as a hard fail.

p.u: One emphasis rule, because bold means three different things
p.x: One emphasis rule, because bold means three different things. Draft writers have one emphasis tool in Word, so bold arrives carrying three different intents. Treating them identically, the earlier behaviour, turned every screen into a field of pills. The rule separates them: a drug or molecule name is an entity and takes a tag; a therapeutic area is a descriptor and stays in the sentence as inline bold; a placeholder takes a tag with its brackets visible, so dynamic content reads as dynamic; instructional words like CURRENTLY and DO NOT take inline bold; line-of-therapy notation and generic phrases take nothing. It also caps itself: one or two indications in bold per screen, and more than six drug tags means the layout is wrong, not the rule. One divergence is still open, and the skills say so. The rule asks for an entity tag visibly different from a placeholder tag; on the frozen screens both are the same light monospace tag, told apart only by the brackets. The skills follow the screens, because the screens are the source of truth, and the call is flagged as mine to make.
The screens are the design; this is the machinery that holds them steady from one boilerplate to the next and one run to the next.

p.u: Decision 1: An orchestrator with specced sub-agents, not one clever session
p.x: Decision 1: An orchestrator with specced sub-agents, not one clever session. The orchestrator became a conductor: it runs the pipeline, holds the human conversation, spawns sub-agents and reads their short reports, and never does the heavy work itself, so its context stays lean. Three sub-agents (brief writer, designer, evaluator) each run in their own context window and are defined as files, with their model, tools, scope and persona declared once. Because each is specced once and reused, the designer behaves identically across every boilerplate and every run. Tradeoff: more moving parts and a real specification burden up front, in exchange for runs that are repeatable instead of merely successful. Parallel designers also multiply token cost per minute, the win is wall-clock time and clean context, not spend.

p.u: Decision 2: Scope each agent's knowledge asymmetrically
p.x: Decision 2: Scope each agent's knowledge asymmetrically. Who gets which skill became a design decision rather than a configuration detail. The brief writer gets the draft-parsing and study-type knowledge. The designer gets the tokens, the composition rules and the brand-asset server. The evaluator gets the same tokens and canonical screens, so it grades against the same target the designer aimed at, plus the rubric and a set of "look out for" criteria the designer never sees, on a different model. Tradeoff: the asymmetry costs duplication and makes the system harder to explain. It is the only thing keeping the review honest.

p.u: Decision 3: A rubric with non-negotiables, not a verdict
p.x: Decision 3: A rubric with non-negotiables, not a verdict. The evaluator scores each dimension 0, 1 or 2 and must attach an actionable critique to anything below a 2. A screen passes only when no dimension scores zero and source-text fidelity and emphasis correctness each score a full 2. Those two are correctness, not quality: the visible text must be an in-order subsequence of the source, with nothing added, removed, reordered or rephrased. The remaining dimensions: typography and token compliance, cohesion with the canonical screens, illustration relevance, and consistency with the screens already approved in that run, can carry a partial. Tradeoff: a rigid gate will fail work a human would have waved through. That is the point: the alternative is "only trivial nitpicks", which is how the first version let bad screens pass.

The architecture, problem by problem. The rebuild started from a written architecture, and its first table is a list of eight things wrong with the version that worked. Every part of the new pipeline answers one of them. What was wrong What it caused What the rebuild does 1 · One context window did everything On long runs the window blew out and the model emitted nonsense. An orchestrator that only conducts, and three sub-agents with a context window each. 2 · No real agent files Sub-agents were improvised at runtime, so behaviour drifted from run to run. Each agent is a file, specced once: model, tools, scope, persona, skills. 3 · A linear pipeline About 30 minutes and 110k tokens for 7 to 10 boilerplates. One designer per boilerplate, in parallel, with evaluation pipelined behind them. 4 · The strongest model on rote work Identification and file creation ran slow and expensive. Sonnet for brief writing and evaluation; Opus for the design itself. 5 · A subjective evaluator “Only trivial nitpicks” let bad output pass. A rubric with thresholds and two non-negotiables.

6 · A second scoring pass after the loop Two evaluators, one of them checking what the other ignored. One evaluator, holding every check. 7 · Designer and evaluator on the same criteria The evaluator rubber-stamped the designer. Evaluator-only rubric and look-out-for criteria, on a different model. 8 · Draft to markdown by reasoning A solved conversion treated as a model task. A deterministic script, no model at all. Parallel designers raise one more problem: each one makes its own choices, and a survey’s screens could drift apart. It is solved upstream rather than by going back to one designer: rigid skills with the eight screens as a shared target, the same designer spec for every boilerplate, one overall brief every designer reads, and an evaluator that catches what is left. The input stays the Word draft the SPI team already has, and business context comes from the brief writer’s persona, a pharmaceutical market research expert, rather than a skill nobody could have written yet.

Where the humans stand. Two gates, both deliberate. The first is after classification: a human confirms which boilerplates are in scope before anything is designed, because the cheapest error to fix is a screen that should never have been drafted. The second is after the loop: a human reviews the finished screens and, if they are wrong, says so in plain language, and the orchestrator re-enters the loop with that feedback as context. The outer loop is written into the orchestrator rather than left to the person's initiative.

p.u: What the system refuses to do
p.x: What the system refuses to do. A sizeable set of boilerplates is deliberately out of scope: consent and privacy screens, anything ending in a yes/no attestation, adverse-event terminology, screen-in and screen-out copy, welcome and post-survey screens. These are detected and skipped rather than attempted. Knowing what not to automate was as much of the design work as the rest.

p.u: Honest limits on what I can claim
p.x: Honest limits on what I can claim. The outcome I can claim is the process change: three teams and around seven days became the SPI team alone and about an hour. Those are approximate figures, as the team reports them, with no usage analytics behind them yet. Everything else here is reasoning I can show: the corpus counts, the old version's costs as the baseline, and the output format checked against the live platform.

Learnings I've taken forward. Design first, derive second: a rule set extracted from text asserts opinions nobody has reacted to. Design the screens, then write the rules the screens imply. Automation does not remove design judgement; it relocates it. Every decision a designer would normally make per screen has to be made once, in advance, and written down precisely enough for a machine: what emphasis means, when an illustration is allowed, what "good" scores. The rubric is the design work. And a system that reviews itself needs that review to be genuinely adversarial (different model, different criteria, scorecard not verdict) or it will simply agree with itself.

Business travellers were ready to move: The agency’s case study describes them as willing to leave the car for alternative mobility, with the app positioned to help change travel habits, and administration and mobility costs managed in the same place. Two users, one home screen: The daily commuter and the occasional traveller need the same first question answered fast: where to, and by what. Goals: Convenience and control: Let people book any available mode of transport and stay in charge of their journey. Seamless mobility: One application that serves daily commuters and on-the-go users alike. One sign-on, every carrier: An overview of the available carriers behind a single sign-on, planning through booking.

Key decisions: “Hi, where to?” is the whole home screen: The home asks one question. From and To, the saved home and work addresses underneath, and a bar with Plan, Near me, Bookings and More: planning is the default, everything else is a tab. Travel options as comparable rows: Each option is one row: departure and arrival, duration, price, and the chain of modes as icons, bike to train to tram, so a commuter compares by time or by money at a glance. Opening one gives the leg-by-leg route, with the ticket purchase inline on the leg that needs it. Tickets without leaving the app: Buying a train ticket is one short form: the off-peak discount toggle, class, trip type, payment method, the price, one button. E-tickets and flexible payment were on the feature list; the design keeps them to a single screen. Near me, by mode: A map filtered by mode, public transport, scooter, bike or car, with each nearby vehicle shown with its distance, plate and battery level, and the nearest station’s next departures. A vehicle’s own page carries its provider, address and the handover to the provider’s app where that was still needed.

What the app does: Mobility-as-a-Service: Public transport and shared e-bikes, scooters and cars, booked from one account. Travel and trip planner: Door to door across modes, with the return trip planned from the same screen. Nearby place explorer: Stations, stops and shared vehicles around the user, on the map. Real-time location tracking: The live position on the route; the app asks for location services only when it needs them. Smart expense management: Administration and mobility costs handled in the app, for business travellers. E-tickets and flexible payment: Tickets bought and held in the app, paid the way the user prefers. Easy ridesharing: Shared rides alongside the carriers, from the same planner.

How it was built, per the agency: Information gathering and analysis: the app’s requirements and goals, collected before anything was drawn. Design and development: wireframes and prototypes for the interface and the experience, then the build in React Native on a Node.js and PostgreSQL back end. Integration of the mobility features: location services and real-time tracking among them. Testing and quality assurance before release. Outcome: What shipped is the one-app idea: plan, compare, book and pay across carriers, in Dutch and English, for the commuter and the on-the-go traveller alike. The agency’s case study states no figures for it, so I claim none. Honest limits: Agency work, 2020 to 2022; the client’s own data stayed with the client. Everything here follows the agency’s published case study and the screens.

Raftaarr (B2B Marketplace). Raftaarr is an online marketplace where industrial micro, small and medium enterprises trade used machinery. Companies list machines with specifications and pictures, post what they need, build a portfolio of their work and run several business profiles from one account, while a feed of posts and ad banners keeps buyers and sellers talking. Appventurez built the app and the website; I led the design of both. Client: Raftaarr, a subsidiary of Electronica Finance Limited Users: Industrial micro, small and medium enterprises, as sellers and buyers Role: Sr. UI/UX Designer at Appventurez, the agency that built it Timeline: 2022 – 2023 Built with: Angular, Node.js, React Native Design tools: Figma, Jira, Bugzilla, Adobe Photoshop

The problem: The brief, in the agency’s words, was a user-friendly platform where people buy and sell online easily, in three parts: a one-stop platform with an intuitive interface where sellers list products or share their interests; interactive community engagement, with posts for insights, industry updates and achievements; and seamless communication, meaning 24/7 customer support, prompt answers to inquiries and channels between industrial MSMEs and their customers. Underneath sat the harder question. A used lathe is not a pair of shoes: a buyer wants its specification, its history and some reason to trust the seller before a single call is made, and a seller with nothing to sell this month still needs a reason to open the app. How does a marketplace for second-hand machinery feel trustworthy enough that a small company lists a machine on it, and lively enough that it comes back when it has nothing to sell?

Two reasons to open the app: A seller comes to list, a buyer to search. Both need a reason to return in between, which is what the requirement posts, the portfolios and the community feed are for. A company is not one person: Companies create and manage multiple profiles from the core panel of the app, and admins tailor profiles to business segments, so one account can speak for several lines of business. Speed, in two colours: Raftaar means speed. The logo pairs the name with line elements that suggest forward motion, and the brand pairs orange, for energy, with blue, for trust. Goals: Unified experience: The same ease of use on the app and the website. Efficient discovery: Advanced search so people find exactly the machines they need. Community interaction: Posts and responses that let users communicate and collaborate.

Key decisions: A listing is a machine profile, not a classified ad: Each machine carries its specifications, pictures and description, with the seller’s verification shown on the card and the price in rupees up front, so a buyer can judge before the first call. Requirements are first-class: A buyer posts what it needs the same way a seller posts what it has. The marketplace works in both directions, and a requirement is as visible as a listing. A portfolio next to the catalogue: Sellers show their achievements, collaborations and the impact of their machinery solutions alongside the products themselves, which is what turns a list of machines into a company worth calling. The dashboard shows money, not metrics: The first thing a seller sees is payable against paid, month by month, with a duration picker. For a small business the question is cash, not clicks. Promotion and community share one scroll: Admin-created ad banners sit in the same feed as company posts and achievements, so a wireless-speaker offer and a precision-gear milestone pass under the same thumb.

What the platform does: Product showcase and requirement posting: Detailed machinery profiles with specifications, pictures and descriptions; requirements posted alongside. Portfolio building: Sellers showcase products with achievements, successful collaborations and the impact of their machinery solutions. User profile management: Companies create and manage multiple profiles from the core panel; admins tailor profiles to business segments. Community posts: Insights, industry updates and achievements, with responses, on app and website. Support and communication: 24/7 customer support, prompt answers to inquiries, and channels between MSMEs and their customers. Advanced search: Search by specific criteria, the same on the app and the website. Interactive ad banners: Created by admins, placed in the feed.

UI/UX design for easy navigation by both sellers and buyers, the part I led. End to end: front end and back end, community engagement, user authentication, security and customisation. Click it by Holcim (B2B Ordering). Click it is the app Holcim and Lafarge customers use to order cement and building materials: place an order at any hour, follow the delivery, keep the company account in view and reach customer service, in English and Arabic. Holcim’s MAQER team built it; Appventurez, where I was a senior UI/UX designer, designed the interface, and the job was a redesign of an ordering platform customers already used, not a blank page. Client: Holcim Group, formerly LafargeHolcim Users: Concrete buyers, construction crews and builders: the companies that order cement by the ton Role: Sr. UI/UX Designer at Appventurez, which designed the UI/UX; Holcim’s MAQER team built the app Timeline: 2021 – 2022 Platform: iOS and Android app and a website, in English and Arabic Design tools: Figma, Jira, Adobe Photoshop; the agency also lists Adobe XD, Sketch, UX Pin and Slack

The problem: A building-materials customer is a company, not a person. An owner, a store manager, a salesperson and a payer share one account and one credit line with Holcim, and they order cement by the ton for sites that need it on a given day. The platform they used already existed; the site still tells customers with a Navendor account to get the app. The brief was to redesign it into one app that works for all of those people, in English and Arabic, with bulk orders and deliveries scheduled by truck and train. The agency’s case study names three challenges: an interface that works seamlessly for every kind of user; an app and a website in English and Arabic that stay easy in both; and support for bulk orders and for scheduling deliveries by train and truck, with shipping as a possible later mode. How do you make ordering fifty tons of cement for Tuesday as easy as ordering a book, for four different people on the same company account?

It was a redesign, not a blank page: Customers had accounts, habits and open orders on the old platform. The agency’s case study calls the job redesigning an existing platform; the account stayed, the experience changed around it. A company account has several hands on it: Owner, Store Manager, Salesperson, Payer and View Only are the roles the app ships with. Each person gets what the job needs: a payer lives in the settlement, a salesperson places and reorders. Cement is sold by the bag and ordered by the ton: The product page prices a 50 kg bag including VAT; the cart takes the order in tons; the delivery is loaded onto a numbered truck at a named plant. The screens keep all three units honest at once. Two languages, one structure: English and Arabic meant every layout had to survive mirroring, so the hierarchy could not rely on reading direction. The agency delivered both sets of designs.

Goals: Streamlined procurement: An intuitive app covering orders, account balances and payments. Full visibility: Clear views of orders, deliveries, payment history and performance. Easier communication: Requests and complaints raised, linked to their order and answered in the app.

Key decisions: The home opens on money, then orders: Credit amount with Details, outstanding amount with Pay, then active orders and favourite orders. For a business customer the relationship with Holcim is a credit line, so it comes first; the messages widget above it carries alerts and promotions. Status has a colour and a word: In transit is amber, New is blue, a cleared invoice is green, a credit note is blue, a pending query and a payment due date are red. The same small vocabulary runs through orders, settlement and the help centre, so a store manager reads a screen before reading it. A delivery is a truck from a plant: An order’s page lists each delivery with its map and a timeline, New, Confirmed, Loading, In transit, and under it the loading number, the plant and the truck number, which is what a site foreman asks for on the phone. In Nigeria the trucks themselves are tracked live. Mode of delivery is a first-class choice: Delivery, Pick-up or FCA are the tabs at the top of the cart, and the mode sits on every order card as MOD, beside the LPO and the total, because the same order means different work depending on who moves it. Reorder beats search: A past order is duplicated with one button, and the five most-used product and location combinations sit on the dashboard as favourites. A cement customer orders the same thing to the same site, often. Sign in with the phone: Login takes the registered phone number with its country code, or an email, with Google, LinkedIn, Facebook and Apple as alternatives. The people ordering are on sites, not at desks.

The designs, feature by feature: Ordering and reordering: Place an order at any hour, from anywhere; duplicate a past order with Reorder; the top five product and location combinations are one tap away. The cart shows the ship-to, the remaining balance, each line in tons and the subtotal before checkout. Delivery tracking: Deliveries followed in real time with the important delivery details in view. In Nigeria, the trucks themselves are tracked live. Each delivery carries its map and its timeline, with the loading number, the plant and the truck number. Dashboard: The messages widget so nothing is missed, special promotions, active orders at a glance, and Favourite Orders for the five most-used combinations, straight from the dashboard. Account and statements: The company’s finances under control: complete financial transparency in the app, a monthly statement on request, and filters to find a record quickly. Requests and complaints: Create a complaint or a request, link the order it concerns for faster processing, get the answer from customer service, and filter by status. Users and roles: Account owners add and remove users as needed and assign a predefined role: Owner, Store Manager, Salesperson, Payer or View Only, each switched on or off from the Users list.

How it was designed, per the agency: Research and discovery: understanding what the users required. Ideation and concepts: feature ideas and the first wireframes. Information architecture: navigation flows and the hierarchy of information. Design and wireframing: UI elements aligned with Holcim’s identity, in English and in Arabic. User testing: usability testing with real users, then testing and quality assurance. Deployment as a phased rollout, and post-launch evaluation on feedback and KPIs. Outcome: Click it is live on the App Store and Google Play, operated by Holcim and Lafarge and built by Holcim’s MAQER team. The agency’s case study records designs delivered in English and Arabic, multiple wireframes, and an interface that supports bulk orders and deliveries scheduled by truck, train and other transport; it quotes Holcim’s digital lead on the team’s agility through the complexity of redesigning an existing platform. No figures are published, so I claim none.

EFL Clik (Business Loans). EFL Clik is the mobile app of Electronica Finance Limited (EFL), an Indian non-banking lender with three decades behind it, 200+ branches, 2,000+ employees and assets under management past ₹5,000 crore, that finances micro, small and medium businesses. A business owner picks a loan, applies, hands over documents, sees a credit score and follows the application from a phone; EFL’s own staff sign in to the same app. Appventurez built it, and I designed it. Client: Electronica Finance Limited (EFL) Users: Micro, small and medium businesses applying for loans, and EFL’s own staff Role: Sr. UI/UX Designer at Appventurez, the agency that built it Timeline: 2022 – 2023; launched October 2023 Platform: iOS and Android app and a web portal Built with: Flutter and Dart on Node.js, SQL, Apache and AWS Design tools: Figma; the agency also lists Adobe XD

The problem: A small business that needs a machine or working capital cannot afford a slow loan. Applying has meant paperwork, a branch visit and a long wait, with little view of where the application stands. EFL wanted its customers to do the whole thing from a phone, at any hour, and to trust what they see there; it also wanted its own team in the portal, so the product had an interface for EFL’s staff as well as for its clients. The agency’s case study names three hard parts: document verification and data security, because loan processing needs KYC checks, financial analysis and verified documents and the data is sensitive; scalability, because EFL is growing; and integration with banking systems, fintech APIs and large data sources, which is slow and complex work. How does a loan that used to mean a folder of paper and a branch visit become something a shop owner finishes on a phone, and still feel safe enough to upload an Aadhaar card into?

Two kinds of user, one door: The welcome screen asks User or Employee before anything else. The customer applies and tracks; the employee works the cases. The agency describes it as interfaces for EFL’s admin team and its clients in one platform. Documents are the application: KYC, financial analysis and document verification are the work of a loan. Aadhaar, PAN, address proof, ITR and bank details live in the profile, uploaded once and reused, so the second application is shorter than the first. A number people understand: A credit score of 830 says Excellent in green, with the co-applicant’s and guarantor’s scores beside it. EFL’s blog says the CIBIL score can be generated from a PAN card alone. Ten products, one flow: Machine loans, secured and unsecured business loans, working capital, rooftop solar, loan against property, MSME, SME and emerging-enterprise loans all go through the same page: a brief, the benefits, the USP, Apply.

Goals: Apply from anywhere: A loan application a business owner can complete on a phone. Less paperwork: Documents handed over once, digitally. Always know where you stand: Eligibility, loans and account details visible without a call or a visit.

Key decisions: A guided application: Each loan product has its own page: a brief of the product, its benefits and its USP, with Apply fixed at the bottom. The application then moves step by step, Next after Next, with the one button always in the same place. Documents, once: Identity and address documents are uploaded into the profile, Aadhaar, PAN and address proof, with ITR and a bank account as the next slots, and kept there for the next application. Answers on screen: The eligible amount comes back as a plain sentence and a number; the credit score as a gauge with a word; active and closed loans sit on the home with their amount and date, each loan with its EMIs and overdues. Blue carries the brand, charcoal carries the action: EFL’s blue is the ground of every header and of the cards that matter, the score and the eligible amount. The one thing to do next is a charcoal pill, Next or Apply, so it reads the same on blue and on white. Help lives in the menu: Report Query, Help and Contact Us sit in the More menu with Change Password, Location and Notifications, Terms, Privacy, About Us and Logout; Delete account is one tap further, where it should be findable.

The designs, screen by screen: Welcome and user type: The logo, then one question: User or Employee. Continue stays dim until one is chosen. Profile and documents: Personal details with Aadhaar, PAN and address proof kept in one place. Loan product page: A brief of the product, its benefits and its USP, with Apply fixed at the bottom. Eligibility result: A clear answer: the amount the applicant is eligible for, then the next step. Credit score: The applicant’s score as a gauge with a word, last updated date, and the co-applicant’s and guarantor’s scores beside it. Help and account: The More menu: Profile, Help, Change Password, Location and Notifications, Report Query, Terms, Privacy, About Us, Contact Us and Logout, with Delete account at the end.

How it was built, per the agency: A tailored fintech platform: interfaces for EFL’s admin team and for its clients, with the full loan process streamlined. Streamlined processing: automation that speeds approvals and disbursements and cuts manual work. Secure record management: a document system for submitting and verifying financial documents, with APIs for data security and regulatory compliance. Flutter and Dart on a Node.js, SQL, Apache and AWS back end. Outcome: EFL Clik launched in October 2023 on Google Play and the App Store. EFL’s own blog, in April 2024, presents it as a one-click loan application with real-time status updates, in-app customer service, a CIBIL score from a PAN card alone, EMIs and overdue payments viewed and paid in the app, and loans and documents kept in one place. The agency’s case study quotes EFL’s head of IT and systems on the team’s goal-oriented strategies and attention to detail, from the start of the project to the launch. Neither publishes figures, so I claim none.

Curie.md (Healthtech · AI). Curie.md is ZoomRx's answer to a problem every clinician has: stay current, with no time to do it. It turns the day's healthcare news into multi-source briefs that can be cleared in minutes, with deep-dive articles where a story deserves one, podcasts, quick medical word games and a weekly newsletter around them, personalised to specialty and, one level deeper, to indication. I designed the product: its personalised content architecture and its mobile-first learning journeys, informed by research with healthcare professionals. Role: Senior Product Designer, ZoomRx Scope: Content architecture, learning journeys, end-to-end UX Platform: Mobile-first web and app Status: Live at curie.md The problem: Clinicians are obligated to stay current and structurally denied the time to do it. Medical news is scattered across dozens of sources, written long, and rarely filtered for what this specialist actually needs. The staying-current happens or it does not, and mostly it does not.

The constraint is not motivation. It is time and relevance: a clinical day offers minutes, not sessions, and generic medical news fails the relevance test, because an oncologist has no time for cardiology headlines either. Relevance had to be built in per clinician, and the reading had to fit the minutes the day actually gives. How do you keep a clinician current in the minutes their day actually gives them? Minutes are the currency: Every surface bets on time given back. Briefs compress several sources into one scan, the header counts the minutes saved, and even the games pitch themselves honestly: a few minutes between patients and you are back in the zone. Specialty isn't personal enough: An oncologist and a dermatologist need different news, but so do two oncologists working different indications. Personalisation had to go two levels deep, with stories and topics followable one by one.

Trust needs receipts, and real faces: A summarised brief asks to be believed, so every brief carries its sources one tap away. And a clinician community is only credible if the people in it are real, which is why identity is verified rather than just registered. Goals: Respect the gap: Content that fits the time a clinician actually has, not the time an editor imagined. Personal beyond specialty: Relevance tuned to indications and followed topics, not just the job title. Earn the trust: Sources visible, identity verified where it matters.

Key decisions: A brief is built from many sources, not one headline: Instead of aggregating links, each brief is an AI-composed summary across sources, seven where seven exist, with an "Inside:" hook and a dive-in article when the story warrants depth: a summary box, a "Why it matters" section tabbed by audience so a clinician, a regulatory expert, a researcher and a patient-engagement reader each find their own stake, key metrics shown one at a time to keep density down, and real quotes.: summarising the news means owning the summary. The design answer is transparency: sources always one tap away, never buried. Cards that know how much time you have: Content is typed by time budget: Big Picture for the day's one story, Catch-up for "missed a week?", Deep-Dive, Podcast, Game, so a clinician picks by the minutes they have rather than by scrolling luck. The home was explored twice around this: a stacked-tiles version for variety, and a single-tile swiping version for focus.: archetypes are an editorial promise, every card type has to be filled, every day. Follow the story, not just the feed: News is ongoing, so a developing story can be followed as a story, with updates as it develops, and every article's related topics are followable individually. Personalisation becomes something the reader assembles tap by tap, not a settings page they will never visit.: granular following splinters the content per reader, the feed still has to feel full for a clinician following three narrow topics. Anonymous first, verified when it matters: No registration wall: everything reads logged out, and sign-up is asked only at moments of demonstrated value, the third topic you follow, the comment you try to post. For the community itself, registration is not enough: clinicians find their record, verify their identity, then join the discussion. When sign-in does come, it is a magic link: an email address and one click in the inbox, no password to invent.: anonymous-first delays the sign-up metric on purpose. The bet is that an account created at a moment of value outlasts ten created at a gate.

Designed for stolen minutes: A product that refuses to become noise: Notifications offer exactly two frequencies: once a day, or off. Nudges appear at value moments, never as interruptions to reading. Sessions that end cleanly: Load more if you want, leave if you are done, and the header counts the minutes saved today. One platform, every gap: Briefs for the two-minute check, the dive-in for the ten-minute story, podcasts for the commute, games for the waiting room, the newsletter for the week, the same clinician, met at whatever minute their day offers. Resumable by design: Bookmarks and history keep every path resumable, and desktop and mobile web carry the whole experience.

Validation and iteration: Two home directions, each with its rationale written beside it, variety-first stacked tiles against a focus-first single tile with swipe gestures, and the swipe version taken to a working prototype in iOS Safari, judged in the hand rather than from stills. Three placements explored for bookmarks and history (segmented control, floating pills, bottom-sheet toggle) before one won. The dive-in page rebuilt section by section, each change annotated with its reason: the audience-tabbed "Why it matters", the one-metric-at-a-time tabs, the in-place sources reveal.

Outcome: What the design delivers is visible in the product's own shape: a clinician can arrive anonymous, clear the day's relevant news in minutes, go deep only where it matters, and leave, with the platform quietly counting the minutes it gave back. Curie is live at curie.md as an ecosystem of briefs, podcasts, games and a newsletter. Curie runs as its own brand, separate from ZoomRx’s market-research business, for an audience of healthcare professionals; design was a critical contributor to building the curie.md site, and engagement has been growing fast since. Honest limits: ZoomRx work; specific performance data stays internal. This covers the design reasoning at the level I can share. What I took forward: When your user's scarcest resource is time, the product's job is to give some back, and to say so. Curie prints its value in its own header. And personalisation worth having is assembled by the user in taps, a follow here and a specialty there, never demanded through a settings page.

Clear.bio (Digital Health). Clear.bio is a Dutch digital health company that helps people with type 2 diabetes see how food affects their blood sugar. Its app brings readings from a glucose sensor together with a food diary, so the link between a meal and its effect becomes visible. Appventurez built the app with Clear, and it is one of the projects from my time there as Lead Designer. Role: Lead Designer, Appventurez Client: Clear.bio, Amsterdam Platform: iOS, Android and a web dashboard Built with: Flutter, Python, Angular, MySQL The problem: People with type 2 diabetes are asked to change how they eat, but they rarely see what a particular meal does to their blood sugar. Glucose readings and food notes sit in different places, and raw glucose data is hard to read. Clear wanted both in one app, explained clearly enough to act on.

Goals: Everything in one place: Health, nutrition and glucose information collected in a single app. Data people can read: Analytics presented so users get a clear picture of their health. Timely nudges: Flexible, real-time notifications that keep daily routines on track. The solution: One timeline: Meals, activity and glucose share a single curve for the day, so cause and effect sit side by side. A score for every meal: Each meal is translated into a score, its glucose peak and the change it caused: one glance instead of a chart to decode. Help at the right moment: A nutrition expert is one tap away from any score, and reminders with flexible settings keep the routine going.

The designs: Logging a meal: Choose food or drink, the time and the type of meal, then add a new meal or reuse a recent one. The day at a glance: The glucose curve for the day with meals and activity marked on it, and every entry listed below with its score. Health in numbers: Time in target range, number of peaks and average blood sugar, above the day's glucose chart. Glucose response per meal: Each meal gets a score, its glucose peak and the change it caused, with the curve that followed. Chat with a nutrition expert: A question about a score goes straight to a nutrition expert inside the app. Practitioner dashboard: A web view for the care team: each member's overview, logged data, food scores, weekly reports and notes. Outcome: The flows were settled with interactive prototypes and A/B tests. The app shipped with diet, fitness and health tracking, nutrition planning and real-time health reports, and Clear's Head of Tech said the Appventurez team delivered on time and built their feedback into the product.

Zena (Conversational Support). A support agent inside the MR Survey App. When a survey link breaks or a bonus is late, a panelist asks Zena from the point they are stuck; it finds the survey, answers what it can, and turns the rest into a ticket with the conversation attached. Designed and vibe-coded by me. Role: Senior Product Designer, ZoomRx Platform: Web, inside the MR Survey App dashboard Related: MR Survey App case study The problem: Panelists’ problems used to arrive as emails and as comments in the End-of-Survey Feedback: a survey link that would not open, a bonus that had not shown up, a question about the account. Each one went to the community team to sort out by hand, usually without the detail needed to act on it. The feedback data from the NPS system already said which questions repeat, so the cases Zena opens with are the ones panelists actually raise.

Goals: Report a break where it happens: A survey that fails should be reported from the dashboard, with the survey identified, not described from memory in an email. Answer the recurring questions live: Payments, bonuses, referrals and technical issues, in the panelist’s own words, at any hour. Hand off cleanly: Anything Zena cannot settle becomes a ticket for the team, with a summary and an ID the panelist can keep.

What Zena does: Starts from the common cases: It opens with the asks that recur most as one-tap options (referrals, technical issues, a survey link not working, why use the app) and a free text box for everything else. Finds the survey for you: Asked which survey is giving trouble, it searches the panelist’s own survey list and confirms the survey and its status before doing anything. Creates the ticket itself: When it cannot fix the problem it files a support ticket, tells the panelist the ticket ID and the response window, and keeps “Get support from our team” one tap away throughout. Knows the payment rules: For a bonus still under review it explains the review window from the completion date, offers to flag the payment for investigation, and opens that ticket too. Outcome: Built inside the panelist dashboard, where the problems happen, and shown in the recording above. Ticket-deflection and first-contact-resolution numbers are not collected yet, so none are claimed here.

Media Tracking (Media Measurement). Media Tracking is ZoomRx’s measurement of pharma advertising as verified physicians and patients actually meet it. Two products, a Digital Tracker and a TV Tracker, passively capture each panelist’s ad exposures across search, banners, email, healthcare sites, linear TV and streaming, and now the medical answers AI tools give, then ask the same people what they recalled. Pharma marketing teams use it to see what their spend and their competitors’ spend is doing. I contributed product design to it as part of ZoomRx’s design team. Product: Digital Tracker (launched 2021) and TV Tracker (2023), one Media Tracking team since 2024 Users: Pharma brand, media and omnichannel teams Panel: Verified HCPs and patients from ZoomRx’s own panel, opted in, no personal data captured Role: Senior Product Designer, ZoomRx design team

The problem: Digital and TV are two of the largest lines in a pharma marketing budget, after the field force, yet most measurement of them is modelled from pixels or panels of general consumers and arrives months late. A brand team cannot tell whether its banner reached oncologists or just impressions, or what a competitor ran last week. How do you turn a passive stream of one physician’s ad exposures into something a brand team can act on in a fortnight? Person-level beats modelled: Every participant is a confirmed HCP or patient, so share of voice and targeting efficiency are measured on the people who matter, not estimated. Observe, then ask: Phase one captures real exposures and the competitive landscape; phase two surveys the same panelists on recall, brand lift and intent, so behaviour and perception sit side by side. AI answers are a channel now: Physicians increasingly get medical answers from Google’s AI Overviews and chat tools instead of clicking links; the tracker records those answers too.

What it captures: Paid search: The queries physicians run, competitor ad copy, the keywords that trigger it and where it lands. Banners and email: Endemic and non-endemic display, static and video; manufacturer, rep and third-party email. Healthcare browsing: Sites visited, content read and time on site. Med AI: The responses AI tools give physicians, captured like any other exposure. TV, linear and streaming: Ad exposure identified by audio fingerprinting; person-level share of voice across both. Competitor creative: The actual emails, banners and commercials competitors ran, as they ran them. Outcome: Media Tracking is live and sold to pharma brands, with insights delivered every two weeks rather than the months-later reports of modelled measurement.
